content.text: Intake (new patient) — New vs established:
a new patient has had no professional services from you, or from another physician of the same specialty in the same group practice, within the previous 3 years.
Intake (new patient) — Medical history (Medicare's minimum list):

past medical and surgical history (illnesses, hospital stays, operations, allergies, injuries, treatments); current medications and supplements, including calcium and vitamins; family history, including diseases that may be hereditary or raise the patient's risk.
Intake (new patient) — Social history (Medicare's minimum list):
alcohol, tobacco and illicit drug use; diet; physical activities.
Progress / follow-up — Progress:
document the patient's progress, response to and changes in treatment, and any revision of the diagnosis.
Progress / follow-up — Problem addressed:

a problem counts as addressed only when you evaluate or treat it at the visit (including considering tests or treatment that end up not chosen, after weighing risk and benefit or by patient choice). Noting that another clinician manages it, without your own assessment or care coordination, does not count.
Annual (routine physical) — Medicare and routine physicals:

Medicare excludes routine physical checkups (exams for a purpose other than treating or diagnosing a specific illness, symptom, complaint or injury), except listed screenings, the initial preventive physical exam and the annual wellness visit.
Medicare wellness (IPPE and AWV) — IPPE timing:
the initial preventive physical examination must be within 1 year after the start of the patient's first Medicare Part B coverage.
Medicare wellness (IPPE and AWV) — IPPE contents:

review of medical and social history (focus on modifiable risk factors); depression risk review with a screening tool; functional ability and level of safety; exam with height, weight, BMI, blood pressure and a visual acuity screen.
Medicare wellness (IPPE and AWV) — IPPE contents, continued:

end-of-life planning if the patient agrees; review of current opioid prescriptions; screening for substance use disorders; education, counseling and referral, including a brief written plan (eg, a checklist) for the screening and preventive services Medicare covers.
Medicare wellness (IPPE and AWV) — Functional ability and safety (minimum):
hearing impairment; activities of daily living; falls risk; home safety.
Medicare wellness (IPPE and AWV) — AWV eligibility:
past the first 12 months of Part B, with no IPPE or AWV in the past 12 months.
Medicare wellness (IPPE and AWV) — First AWV:

review the health risk assessment; establish the medical and family history and a list of the patient's current providers and suppliers; measure height, weight, BMI (or waist circumference) and blood pressure; detect any cognitive impairment.
Medicare wellness (IPPE and AWV) — First AWV, continued:

review depression risk (with a screening instrument) and functional ability and level of safety; set up a written screening schedule (eg, a checklist for the next 5 to 10 years) based on USPSTF and ACIP recommendations, plus a list of risk factors and conditions with interventions recommended or underway.
Medicare wellness (IPPE and AWV) — First AWV, continued:
personalized health advice and referrals; advance care planning at the patient's discretion; review of current opioid prescriptions; screening for substance use disorders.
Medicare wellness (IPPE and AWV) — Health risk assessment:
self-reported, takes no more than 20 minutes, and at minimum covers demographics, self-assessed health status, psychosocial risks, behavioral risks, ADLs and IADLs.
Medicare wellness (IPPE and AWV) — Subsequent AWV:

update the health risk assessment, medical and family history and provider list; measure weight (or waist circumference) and blood pressure; detect cognitive impairment; update the screening schedule and risk-factor list.
Chronic care visit — Stable chronic illness:

expected to last at least one year or until death. "Stable" is judged against the patient's own treatment goals: a patient not at goal is not stable, even if the condition hasn't changed and there's no short-term threat to life or function.
Chronic care visit — Exacerbation or progression:
a chronic illness that is acutely worsening, poorly controlled or progressing, needing added supportive care or attention to treatment side effects.
Chronic care visit — CCM eligibility:
2 or more chronic conditions expected to last at least 12 months or until death, or that place the patient at significant risk of death, acute exacerbation or decompensation, or functional decline.
Chronic care visit — CCM initiating visit:

required for new patients or patients not seen within the previous 1 year: a comprehensive face-to-face E/M visit, AWV or IPPE. If CCM isn't discussed at that visit, it doesn't count as the initiating visit.
Chronic care visit — CCM consent (document it):

get written or verbal consent before billing. Record that you told the patient about CCM's availability, possible cost sharing, that only 1 practitioner can bill CCM in a calendar month, and their right to stop at any time, and whether they accepted or declined.
Chronic care visit — CCM care plan:

a patient-centered electronic comprehensive care plan based on physical, mental, cognitive, psychosocial, functional and environmental assessment and an inventory of resources and supports. It may include a problem list, expected outcome and prognosis, measurable treatment goals, symptom management, planned interventions, medical management, caregiver assessment, coordination with outside resources and practitioners, and periodic review.
